header: THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH, BENCH AT SUKKUR
Respondents No.1 to 6 : 1. Mushtaque Ali 2. Muhammad Hussain 3.
Fakir Muhammad alias Shahid Ali 4. Gulzar
J U D G M E N T
body: TASNEEM SULTANA, J.- The appellant, Muhammad Ayoub Majeedano, has called into question the judgment dated 22.09.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Mirwah, in Crl. Appeal No.12 of 2026, whereby the conviction and sentence of respondent No.1, Mushtaque Ali Depar, recorded by the learned I-Civil Judge and Judicial Magistrate, Mirwah, in Criminal Case No.262 of 2023, arising out of Crime No.180 of 2022 of Police Station Mirwah, were set aside and he was acquitted of the charge. The learned appellate Court also extended the benefit of acquittal to respondents Nos.2 to 6, who had been convicted with respondent No.1.

2. Brief facts of the prosecution case are that on 27.04.2022 at about 7:30 a.m., the appellant was working on his agricultural land when Hussain Bux and six private respondents came there armed with lathis. According to the appellant, Hussain Bux questioned him about cultivating the land and instigated the others to assault him. Hussain Bux struck him with a lathi on a finger of his right hand, while the others gave him blows on his legs and other parts of his body. On his cries, his uncle Wali Muhammad and his cousin Muhammad Punhal came running towards him, whereupon the accused left after obstructing the path with thorny branches. The appellant obtained a letter from Police Post Pir Wassan and received medical treatment. The FIR was registered on 06.11.2022 pursuant to an order dated 03.11.2022 passed on his application for registration of the case.

3. After usual investigation, the police submitted the charge-sheet against Hussain Bux and the six private respondents under Section 173, Crl. Acquittal Appeal No.S-119 of 2026 2 Cr.P.C. The requisite documents were supplied to the accused under Section 241-A, Cr.P.C., whereafter formal charge was framed at Ex.2, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. During trial, Hussain Bux died and the proceedings against him were abated vide order dated 09.09.2024 at Ex.11. An amended charge was thereafter framed against the six private respondents at Ex.12, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Their pleas were recorded at Exs.13 to 18.

4. To prove the charge, the prosecution examined PW-1 Hyder Raza, the investigating officer, at Ex.10, PW-2 Muhammad Ayoub, the injured complainant, at Ex.19, PW-3 Wali Muhammad at Ex.20, PW-4 Mst. Bhagul, mashir of the place of occurrence and injuries, at Ex.21, and PW-5 Dr. Jamal Nasir at Ex.22. The appellant produced the FIR at Ex.19/1 and the order for its registration at Ex.19/2. The medical officer produced the police letter and the provisional and final medical certificates at Exs.22/1 to 22/3. Thereafter, the learned ADPP closed the prosecution side vide statement at Ex.23. In their statements recorded under Section 342, Cr.P.C., at Exs.24 to 29, the private respondents denied the allegations and stated that the witnesses were interested and had deposed falsely against them. They neither examined themselves on oath under Section 340(2), Cr.P.C., nor led any evidence in defence.

5. After hearing learned counsel for the parties, the learned trial Court convicted and sentenced all six private respondents vide judgment dated 11.07.2026. For the offences under Sections 147 and 148 read with Section 149, P.P.C., each was sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the Court and fined Rs.1,000/- for each offence. Each was also sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.1,500/- under Section 341 read with Section 149, P.P.C., and daman of Rs.20,000/- to the appellant under Section 337-F(v) read with Section 149, P.P.C. Respondent No.1, Mushtaque Ali Depar, challenged his conviction and sentence before the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Mirwah, in Criminal Appeal No.12 of 2026. The learned appellate Court allowed the appeal vide judgment dated 22.09.2026, set aside the conviction and sentence of respondent No.1 and acquitted him of the charge. The benefit of acquittal was also extended to respondents Nos.2 to 6, who had not preferred any appeal. The judgment of the learned appellate Crl. Acquittal Appeal No.S-119 of 2026 3 Court has been assailed by the complainant through the instant Criminal Acquittal Appeal.

6. Learned counsel for the appellant contends that the prosecution witnesses had fully supported the complainant’s version and that there was no material contradiction in their depositions; that the learned appellate Court had discarded their evidence without assigning sound reasons, although the oral and documentary evidence on record was sufficient to sustain the convictions; that respondent No.1, Mushtaque Ali Depar, alone had preferred an appeal and sought waiver of daman, yet the learned appellate Court extended the benefit of acquittal to respondents Nos.2 to 6, who had neither challenged their convictions nor sought such relief; that the appeal had been allowed without notice to the appellant and prays that the impugned judgment dated 22.09.2026 be set aside and the convictions and sentences awarded by the learned trial Court vide judgment dated 11.07.2026 be restored.

8. From a perusal of the record, it appears that the learned trial Court relied upon the evidence of PW-2 Muhammad Ayoub, the appellant, and PW-3 Wali Muhammad and concluded that the private respondents had joined Hussain Bux in the assault in prosecution of their common object. The learned appellate Court examined the part attributed to the private respondents in the FIR and in the appellant’s deposition at Ex.19. In the FIR, the appellant alleged that Hussain Bux struck him on a finger of his right hand and that the others gave him blows on his legs and other parts of his body. In his deposition, he stated that all the accused attacked him at the instigation of Hussain Bux. He attributed a specific blow only to Hussain Bux. It was in this context that the learned appellate Court referred to the evidence of PW-5 Dr. Jamal Nasir, the medical officer, at Ex.22, who found a single injury below the little finger of the right hand. The injury recorded by PW-5 was consistent with the lathi blow described by the appellant. PW-5 found no injury on the legs or elsewhere corresponding to the further blows alleged in the FIR.

Crl. Acquittal Appeal No.S-119 of 2026 4 9. PW-3 Wali Muhammad stated that he was working on the adjoining land when the accused came to the land of the appellant and assaulted him. He further stated that when he rushed to the spot, he found the appellant with a broken finger. In cross-examination, he placed himself at a distance of about 500 feet from the place of occurrence. According to the version given by the appellant in the FIR, PWs Wali Muhammad and Muhammad Punhal came running on hearing his cries and the accused left on seeing them. These statements bear directly on the finding of the learned trial Court that Wali Muhammad had witnessed the private respondents taking part in the assault. On reaching the spot, PW-3 Wali Muhammad saw the injury to the finger of the appellant. His evidence, however, leaves doubt as to whether he had seen any of the private respondents take part in the assault before he reached the spot. Both the appellant and Wali Muhammad acknowledged that there was a dispute with the accused over the measurement of the land. A separate blow by each respondent was unnecessary to establish liability under Section 149, P.P.C. On the evidence discussed above, the learned appellate Court had reasonable grounds for doubting whether the six private respondents had joined in the assault. As regards wrongful restraint, the appellant stated that the accused obstructed the path, but gave no particulars of whom they thereby prevented from proceeding. Wali Muhammad gave no account of anyone being stopped.

10. The learned trial Court had convicted all six private respondents on the same evidence, and the grounds on which the learned appellate Court acquitted respondent No.1 applied equally to respondents Nos.2 to 6. As to whether the benefit of acquittal could extend to them in the absence of appeals of their own, the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan in Muhabbat Ali and another v. The State (1985 SCMR 662) held as under:

“As regards the non-appealing convict, Muhammad Ramzan, we direct that the benefit of acceptance of this appeal shall also be extended to him who shall stand acquitted and will be set at liberty forthwith if not required in connection with some other case.”

The learned appellate Court was, therefore, justified in extending the same relief to respondents Nos.2 to 6. The remaining objection concerns the Crl. Acquittal Appeal No.S-119 of 2026 5 absence of notice to the appellant. The learned trial Court had awarded him daman, and the appellate judgment permitted the private respondents to apply for return of the amounts deposited. He therefore had a direct interest in the appeal and ought to have been heard. The question under Section 537, Cr.P.C., is whether that omission occasioned a failure of justice. The appellant seeks restoration of the convictions on the evidence recorded at trial. Learned counsel has been heard on that evidence, and his submissions have been examined above. He has identified no further material or submission which the appellant was prevented from placing before the learned appellate Court. In these circumstances, the absence of notice has not occasioned a failure of justice warranting interference with the impugned judgment.

11. In Muhammad Riaz versus Khurram Shehzad and another (2024 SCMR 51), the Honourable Supreme Court held as under: “10. The aforesaid set of circumstances creates misgivings and suspicions regarding the presence of the prosecution witnesses at the scene of the crime, and the discrepancies and defects in the investigation and the prosecution case pointed out by the learned High Court in the impugned judgment also colors the case in doubt and improbability. Therefore, the learned High Court rightly held that the prosecution badly failed to substantiate the case against the respondent No. 1, and the learned Trial Court was not justified in convicting him on the strength of untrustworthy or uncorroborated evidence which was full of material contradictions, especially contradictions in the ocular and medical evidence. It is a well-settled exposition of law that in an appeal against acquittal, the Court would not ordinarily interfere and would instead give due weight and consideration to the findings of the Court acquitting the accused which carries a double presumption of innocence, i.e. the initial presumption that an accused is innocent until found guilty, which is then fortified by a second presumption once the Court below confirms the assumption of innocence, which cannot be displaced lightly.”

12. In view of the above facts and circumstances, the learned appellate Court was justified in extending the benefit of doubt to the private respondents. The appellant has failed to point out any material misreading or non-reading of evidence in the impugned judgment warranting interference with their acquittal. Consequently, the instant Criminal Acquittal Appeal along with pending application(s), if any, is dismissed. J U D G E Crl. Acquittal Appeal No.S-119 of 2026 6 Ahmad
